The method illustrates the robustness of the average-based scheme to high albedos [S1].

The claim states that the evidence supports the robustness of the average-based scheme to 'high albedos'. However, the evidence in Source [S1] explicitly discusses the performance and robustness of the scheme in the context of 'non-absorbing volumes' (where albedo is 1, which is high) and 'absorbing' scenes. Specifically, the text notes that using a free-path-sampling coefficient that underestimates the extinction bound causes variance to rise abruptly due to fireflies, 'especially in non-absorbing volumes' (high albedo). Furthermore, the analysis of the 'color explosion' scene (which has spectrally varying coefficients) compares average-based and maximum-based schemes, noting that maximum-based probabilities yielded slightly better performance (lower LTUV) than average-based ones. The evidence highlights that the average-based scheme is 'immune to fireflies' when properly bounded, but it also highlights vulnerabilities (variance rise) in non-absorbing (high albedo) scenarios if bounds are not respected, and does not explicitly frame the 'robustness' as a specific strength against high albedos compared to other conditions, but rather focuses on the general bounding property. More critically, the claim implies a specific positive correlation or robustness *to* high albedos that is not the primary conclusion; the text actually warns about issues in non-absorbing (high albedo) volumes if the bounding coefficient is underestimated. Therefore, the evidence does not straightforwardly support the specific claim of robustness to high albedos in the manner suggested, as it identifies high albedo (non-absorbing) as a condition where errors (fireflies) can arise if bounds are violated, and where maximum-based schemes performed better.

It addresses the limitations of naive delta tracking in chromatic media, where independent tracking of wavelengths leads to high variance and fireflies [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that naive delta tracking handles each wavelength independently (Section 5.3). It further explains that local collision weights can exceed 1, leading to geometric growth of path throughput, which causes variance and fireflies (Section 5.1.2 and Discussion). The proposed method addresses these limitations by incorporating path history to bound throughput and suppress noise/fireflies in chromatic media.
